The test image shows corn ears (pods) with a large dark brown/black powdery spore mass on the husks, with orange kernels still visible on the upper ear. This points to a smut disease affecting the ear.

Pod candidates: Head_Smut, Diplodia_Ear_Rot, Gibberella_Disease, Trichoderma_Ear_Rot, Southern_Corn_Leaf_Blight, Tar_Spot.

The dark spore mass replacing ear tissue strongly suggests Head_Smut or Common_Smut. Let me check reference images.
The Head_Smut pod reference (206) closely matches - dark black/brown spore mass inside peeled-back husks on a green plant. Let me check a few more candidates to confirm.

I've now used all 8 reference views across the key candidates. Summary of comparisons:

- **Head_Smut (pod/206)**: Dark black/brown spore mass inside peeled-back husks on green plant — strongly matches the test image
- **Head_Smut (pod/139)**: Later-stage dry plant with dark spore mass inside husk — same disease, different stage
- **Common_Smut (seed/218)**: White-to-black bulging galls on individual kernels — structurally different from test
- **Common_Smut (stem/176)**: Stalk galls with white-silver tissue — different
- **Trichoderma_Ear_Rot**: Green-gray exterior mold on husk — clearly different
- **Diplodia_Ear_Rot**: Exposed yellow kernels with light rot, no spore mass — different
- **Gibberella_Disease**: Pink/white husks — clearly different

The test image shows two ears on a green plant: the upper with exposed orange kernels, the lower with husks peeled back revealing a large dark brown/black spore mass replacing normal ear tissue. This is the classic Head_Smut presentation — a dark spore mass filling the ear cavity where kernels should be, visible when husks are opened. Head_Smut pod reference 206 is nearly identical in setting and appearance.
